canonical_statement: The study evaluated the accuracy and reproducibility of ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 responses to clinician drug-information questions using Lexicomp as the comparison standard.
The investigators conducted a serial cross-sectional evaluation of ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 from March 5 through March 12, 2024.
Trial 1 used 30 real-world pharmacist-oriented drug-information questions, with three questions in each of 10 categories and at least one cardiology-focused question per category.

population.label: Thirty clinician-oriented, real-world drug-information questions spanning 10 categories in trial 1

canonical_statement: The supporting information lists the complete 30-question test set across administration/preparation, contraindications/warnings/precautions, dosage adjustments, dosing, drug interactions, IV compatibility, monitoring, pharmacokinetics, pregnancy/lactation, and adverse-effect categories.

population.label: Thirty clinician-oriented, real-world drug-information questions spanning 10 categories in trial 1

canonical_statement: Two authors searched Lexicomp before the ChatGPT trials to establish the comparison answer and word count for each question.

exposures.details: Commonly accepted drug-information reference used as the study comparison standard

canonical_statement: Each trial-1 question was entered individually into a new chat after clearing the prior history, and the investigators did not ask follow-up questions.
For trials 2 and 3, one question from each category was randomly selected from the original 30 and repeated on days 1 and 7 using the same procedure.

population.label: Ten randomly selected drug-information questions, one per category, repeated on days 0, 1, and 7

canonical_statement: Accuracy was rated on a four-point scale, with scores 3 or 4 classified as accurate and scores 1 or 2 classified as inaccurate for analysis.

outcome.definition: Responses rated 3 or 4 on a four-point accuracy scale were classified as accurate; scores 1 or 2 were classified as inaccurate.
outcome.measurement_method: Independent rating by two clinical pharmacists with third-pharmacist adjudication of discrepancies

canonical_statement: Two clinical pharmacists independently rated each ChatGPT response, a third pharmacist adjudicated disagreements, and the raters were calibrated on four practice questions before data collection.
Reproducibility was defined as consistency in response accuracy across day 0, day 1, and day 7.

concept.text: Reproducibility of response accuracy over time

outcome.definition: Consistency in accuracy across days 0, 1, and 7.
outcome.measurement_method: Pairwise Cohen kappa and Cochran Q across repeated trials

canonical_statement: Usability was assessed with response word counts and a five-question survey completed by the two assessors.

outcome.measurement_method: Five-question survey completed by two assessors using five-point Likert items

canonical_statement: The analysis used McNemar testing for model accuracy comparisons, Cohen kappa for paired-trial agreement, Cochran Q for accuracy over time, chi-square for category and cardiology subgroup comparisons, one-way ANOVA for mean word count, and Kruskal-Wallis testing for median word count.
In trial 1, ChatGPT-3.5 was accurate for 9 of 30 questions (30%) and ChatGPT-4 for 12 of 30 (40%); the model difference was not statistically significant (p=0.51).

canonical_statement: The authors stated that the small number of questions may have left the study underpowered to detect differences between question categories.
The four-point accuracy scale required subjective judgment, although the assessors achieved 100% agreement on calibration questions before data collection.
The five-point assessor survey permitted a neutral response, which the authors noted could bias responses toward the null.
The study used one commonly accepted reference source even though the authors noted that best-practice drug-information work typically uses more than one source.

The authors concluded that ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 had limited accuracy and reproducibility for real-world drug-information questions and advised health care professionals to use caution when relying on ChatGPT for drug information.
The study reported no external funding.
Dr. Cynthia A. Jackevicius reported membership on the JACCP editorial board; the other authors declared no conflicts of interest.
The article states that research data are not shared.
